newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanians get pre-poll winter energy reassurance.
newsitem.headline: Romanians get pre-poll winter energy reassurance.

text.p: Romania has enough fuel reserves for the winter, the Industry Ministry said on Friday, in an apparent pre-election move to reassure voters there will be no repeat of last year's energy crisis.
Industry Ministry director Gavril Georgescu detailed plans to ensure sufficient oil, coal and hydro-power sources for the coming months.
He told a news conference some 7.6 million tonnes of lignite had been stored at power plants. Another 600,000 tonnes were ready for shipment from coalfields, he added.
"Power plants will not face a crisis situation this winter," Georgescu said.

His remarks ahead of Sunday's general elections added to a chorus of reassurance from the authorities in the past month that Romania would not be hit again by the energy crisis which shut down industry and turned off the lights earlier this year.
An acute shortage of hard currency to pay for fuel imports forced the state-run Renel RA electricity authority to cut power supplies to industrial sectors over January-March.
The leftist government of Prime Minister Nicoale Vacaroiu got the blame. Opinion polls now show the ruling Party of Social Democracy trailing behind its main rival.
Romania's power plants produce electricity from a mix of fuels, including oil, gas and coal.
Georgescu said Renel had already secured funds to import fuel oil worth a total $160 million during the cold months.

"One should also add the fuel obtained from the 800,000 tonnes of crude per month we plan to import during the 1996/1997 winter as well as from the 550,000 tonnes of crude extracted locally," Georgescu said, without elaborating.

A $200 million revolving credit arranged with Chase Manhattan would help fund the crude imports. Up to 68 percent of costs for crude imports would be covered by export earnings from processed products, he said.
Romania must import large quantities of crude for domestic energy needs and to keep its refineries operating.

In September the government set up a special fund to finance crude imports. Initially, the central bank tried to squeeze hard currency for crude purchases out of importers and exporters but after opposition it fell back on using credits.
"Our lakes and reservoirs contain enough water to ensure (hydro-electric) production of 2.0 billion kilowatts," he said.
In November, Romania will import some 660 million cubic meters of natural gas which would add to another 624 million already stored in underground facilities, Georgescu said.

Georgescu also said the country's newly-inaugurated nuclear power plant, built on the River Danube with Canadian Candu technology, was expected to add to the national grid some 700 megawatts, or 8.0 percent of Romania's electricity output. -- Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 43120264
